SurfaceVibe: Vibration-Based Tap & Swipe Tracking on Ubiquitous Surfaces

a vibration-based interaction tracking system for multiple surface types
Shijia Pan1 · Ceferino Gabriel Ramirez1 · Mostafa Mirshekari2 · Jonathon Fagert2 · Albert Jin Chung1 · Chih Chi Hu1 · John Paul Shen1 · Hae Young Noh2 · Pei Zhang1

What it is

The paper's story: where it is used, its core idea and the real system demo.
Real-world use

Taps and swipes on an ordinary board, detected by four geophones

Imagine a meeting table where everyone can tap and swipe on the wood itself.

what the four geophones hear

It shows The four geophones' signals after one tap: the wave reaches the nearest one first and the farthest last.

How to read it Time runs to the right and each row is one sensor, its arrival marked: the gaps between the marks tell where the tap was.

drag to turn the space
Office · Sensing World ›
Motivation

Earlier ways to touch large surfaces each have a limit

  1. 1Tabletops and wall surfaces are readily available
  2. 2the interaction area on the device is limited by the device size
  3. 3The vision-based methods are, in general, sensitive to obstructions
  4. 4the dispersion causes high deviation in localization results
an acoustic tracker's tap estimates

It shows Taps at the same marked places, located by arrival times alone: the estimates spread far from each mark.

How to read it Each ring is where a tap really was, and the dots of its colour are where the tracker put it: farther apart is worse.

State of the art

Earlier acoustic ways need training, ignore wave properties, or track no swipes

  1. 1these systems need a large amount of training data
  2. 2existing algorithms that do not take wave properties into account
  3. 3no work has been done on tracking continuous swipe interactions through vibration sensing

It shows Earlier ways and their limits: some must learn each gesture first, and some time the wave but ignore how it travels.

How to read it Each dot is one way and its arrow stops at its limit: no way tracked swipes by vibration before SurfaceVibe.

Background

Four terms used throughout

Geophone01

Geophones (SM-24) detect vibrations caused by surface particles moving perpendicular to the target surface

Time Difference of Arrival, TDoA02

SurfaceVibe calculates the Time Difference of Arrival (TDoA) of event signals detected at different sensors

Dispersion03

different frequency components travel at different speeds in the range of 50 to 300 m/s

Slip pulse04

Since typically static friction is larger than kinetic friction, alternating friction causes a sudden jump in the velocity of the movement, resulting in slip pulse

two geophones, one tap

It shows One tap heard by two geophones: the farther one hears it later, and that delay is the TDoA.

How to read it Time runs to the right, the upper trace is the nearer sensor, and the marked gap is the delay in milliseconds.

a tap's wave as it travels

It shows A tap's wave seen near and far: its frequencies travel at different speeds, so it spreads out as it goes.

How to read it Each row is the wave farther from the tap: the pulse gets longer and its start blurs, and that is dispersion.

a pen sliding: stick and slip

It shows A pen sliding on a surface sticks, then slips: each sudden slip sends out one small pulse.

How to read it Above, the pen's speed over time jumps at each slip; below, the pulse each jump makes in the board.

Core idea

Arrival-time differences at four sensors locate a tap

  1. 1tracks interactions (taps and swipes) through multiple sensors
  2. 2For a pair of sensors, the difference in distances results in a hyperbolic curve
  3. 3the location of their intersection is considered as the source location
the board from above

It shows Each pair of sensors puts the tap on one curve; the curves of all the pairs cross at the tap.

How to read it Squares are the four geophones and the ring is the tap: each curve is one pair's delay, and where they meet is the estimate.

SurfaceVibe's four modules (Fig. 1)

It shows The paper's system in four modules: sensing, telling a tap from a swipe, locating a tap, tracking a swipe.

How to read it The lit box is the module the current line names, and taps end at tap localization while swipes go on to swipe tracking.

Core idea · what to observe

Arrival delays locate a tap and track a swipe

the blue line is leading, meaning the source is closer to Sensor 1Fig. 2(c), the swipe's first segment: the blue line is Sensor 1's signal, and it leads in time of arrival (the shift) because the finger that makes Fig. 2's swipe starts near Sensor 1. Here a pen swipes, as in the paper's tests (§5.1.3).

in the end part of the signal, the shift is reversedFig. 2(e), the swipe's last segment: the finger is now nearer Sensor 2, which detects each slip pulse first. Here a pen swipes, as in the paper's tests (§5.1.3).

  1. A tap: rings spread out from the pen
  2. The nearest geophone detects it first
  3. Measured on the signals, the delays give the curves
  4. They cross near the pen: the tap error is the gap
  5. A swipe: the first sensor to detect moves from S1 to S2
  6. Your turn Drag the pen

How to read it Time runs left to right, in ms after the first peak; each mark is a first peak, and the gaps between marks are the delays. Swipe: 3 ms of each segment, blue S1, red S2; the dot on the left leads.

Challenge 1 · dispersion

Dispersion smears a tap's arrival in time

dispersion introduces distortion, making vibration-based localization a challenge

noise and dispersion make the TDoA unstable when the tap is far from the center

  1. New: the tap's frequencies travel at different speeds
  2. So each arrival is smeared over milliseconds
  3. Read on raw signals, the delays come out unstable
  4. Far from the centre the estimates scatter
  5. Your turn Drag the pen
tap error –
grid scatter –

tap frequencies

It shows One tap at the farthest sensor, then split into three frequency bands: the high band arrives first, so the arrival is smeared.

How to read it Rows: the raw signal, then each band; a red triangle marks each band's arrival; time in ms after the raw arrival.

the board

It shows Each tap's estimate beside the tapped point; from click 3, ten taps at each point of the paper's grid, which scatter far from the centre.

How to read it Rings: the tapped points; dots: the estimates; lines: their centre to the point; circles: their scatter; gold: the four near the centre; red: the rest.

Solution 1 · dispersion

Band and velocity calibration

  1. The system scans through the wavelet scales and finds the scale that gives correct relative locations
  2. the system selects the velocity that minimizes the sum of the localization errors for calibration points
  3. With both, the taps gather on their points
  4. Your turn Calibration off and on; drag the pen

Challenge 2 · reflection

Echoes from the board's edges overlap the direct wave

reflection has a large impact on vibration based sensing

surface sizes may cause different reflection when the margin between sensor and board edge changes

  1. New: each edge sends the wave back
  2. As if a second source stood behind the edge
  3. At a geophone, echoes arrive soon after the direct wave
  4. Over the whole window, echoes shift the delay
  5. Your turn Drag the pen
tap error –

drag it · wheel: 5 mm, Shift finer

echoes

It shows One sensor's raw signal after a tap, and its two parts: the direct wave alone (the same tap with no edges) and the echoes the edges add, on top of it.

How to read it Rows: raw, direct, echoes; time in ms after the direct wave; gold line: the direct wave; dashed red lines: when each edge's echo arrives, named by its edge.

board

It shows The far edge acts like a mirror: an image source behind it sends the echo; read over the whole window, the estimate is pulled off.

How to read it Ring: the tap; gold circle: its wave; dashed red arc: the wave come back from the far edge; red ring: the image behind that edge; red lines: the echo's path, drawn from the pen; gold dot: the estimate.

Solution 2 · reflection

First peak of arrival

  1. the first peak is less likely to be impacted by reflections
  2. The delay between two geophones is read at their first peaks
  3. So the taps stay on their points
  4. Damped edges change little for a tap
  5. Your turn First peak off and on; damped edges too

drag it · wheel: 5 mm, Shift finer

error, grid mean –
grid scatter –

What you saw Each number is this run's mean error over the 16 grid points on wood. With sensors 80 cm apart, taps beyond 20 cm from the centre have up to 18.4 cm average error (§5.2.5). There the first peak decays to the noise.Since the TDoA estimation for tap is based on the first peak of the signal, the reflection reduction does not significantly affect the result

first peak

It shows The nearest sensor's band signal, from click 2 the next one under it: each first peak comes before the echoes, so their delay holds.

How to read it Rings: the tapped points; dots: the estimates, a line from their centre to each point; grey bars: the sand-filled weights, when damped.

Challenge 3 · swipe

A swipe is seconds of friction, not one impulse

the signal often lasts over seconds

When these states are alternating, friction changes between static and kinetic friction

  1. New: the pen slides, sticking and slipping
  2. Each slip sends a pulse into the board
  3. The signal goes on for seconds: no single arrival to time
  4. Which sensor hears first changes as the pen moves
  5. Your turn Drag the pen
S1–S2 delay –

It shows Two sensors over the last seconds: the initial tap's spike, then slip pulses for as long as the pen slides, with no single arrival. At click 2, the slide's last 0.06 s, its pulses one by one.

How to read it Time runs left to right to now; red fill: S2, blue line: S1, each its largest swing per 5 ms; black lines: the segments.

segments

It shows Three 0.02 s pieces of the swipe, at its start, middle and end: the sensor that hears first changes as the pen moves.

How to read it Blue: S1, red: S2, 3 ms of each piece on its time axis; dots: matching peaks, the left one leads.

board

It shows The pen's path on the board, and the one point a tap's method finds: the initial contact, not the swipe.

How to read it Arrow: the pen's path, start to end; gold dot: the initial tap's estimate; S1 and S2: the sensors.

Solution 3 · swipe

Trajectory estimation and initial-tap correction

  1. SurfaceVibe extracts TDoA using cross-correlation from consecutive segments within a swipe and localizes each of them
  2. Each segment gives a point
  3. A line fit gives direction and length
  4. The initial tap corrects the line when they agree
  5. Arbitrary gestures can be approximated by linear swipes and taps
  6. Your turn Correction off and on; a direction

End-to-end

Tap and swipe tracking

Our goal: tap or swipe between the geophones, and see where SurfaceVibe places it.A tap reaches each geophone at a slightly different time. Each pair's time difference puts the tap on one curve, a hyperbola (the coloured lines); the tap is where they cross. A swipe is cut into 0.02 s pieces, each placed the same way; a straight line fits them.

Check the Paper · 2 of 3

Ablation study

Question Which part of SurfaceVibe keeps taps and swipes accurate?The test is the paper's own on the 61 cm wood board: taps at Fig. 3(b)'s 16 points, and swipes in Fig. 3(c)'s eight directions. Each try stays in the two charts, beside all parts on.

You change
SurfaceVibe's parts, one off at a time

drag the pen on the board · the wheel moves it 5 mm, Shift finer

  1. 1Your turn Switch the wavelet band offWith no band, the TDoA comes from the raw signal, where each frequency travels at its own speed. In Fig. 5 the mean tap error on wood is 15 cm with no filter and no calibration. Here the speed is still calibrated.
  2. 2Your turn Fix the speed at 60 m/sThe velocity calibration is off, and the speed stays at the lower bound. Each tap's distance differences come out too small, so the taps land too near the centre, as in Fig. 4(c).
  3. 3Your turn Switch the first peak offThe TDoA then comes from the cross-correlation of the whole window. On undamped edges the echoes fall in that window, and they move the TDoA away from its true value.
  4. 4Your turn Switch the initial tap offA swipe often starts with a tap. When that tap agrees with the swipe's line, SurfaceVibe adds it as one more point, and the swipe reads longer, closer to its true 20 cm.
More controls
Wavelet band
tap error, this try –
swipe length, this try –
tap error at the pen –

What you saw Taps: the mean error at 16 points, 3 taps each (the paper: 10), and of 10 taps at the pen. Swipes: the mean length error of 8 swipes. All on undamped edges, as Fig. 5 and Fig. 10's undamped bars; dashed: their wood, all parts on.The selection of the frequency band to be extracted from the decomposed signal is the key to achieve high accuracy in addition to high precision the estimated locations are skewed inward towards the center due to the underestimated propagation velocity We selected the first peak of arrival since the first peak is less likely to be impacted by reflections the estimated location of the initial tap could be used to further correct the tracking estimation The estimations utilizing calibration on both filtering band and velocity have consistently lower errors than other cases The accuracy of the estimated location shows less than 3cm error

swipe length error of each try, cm

It shows The mean length error of each try's swipes: below zero a swipe reads shorter than its true 20 cm.

How to read it One bar a try, all parts on first, the paper's all-on value dashed; a longer bar downward is a shorter swipe.

Go Beyond the Paper · 1 of 3

Generalization study

Question How far past the paper's tests do SurfaceVibe's taps and swipes stay accurate?The paper tests taps up to 35 cm from the centre (Fig. 6(c)), sensors up to 80 cm apart (Fig. 6(b)) and swipes at 10 cm/s only (§5.1.3). Here the pen goes anywhere on a board up to 121 cm wide, at any speed up to 40 cm/s.

You change
where the pen is, the sensor distance S, the board size B and the swipe speed

drag the pen on the board · the wheel moves it 1 cm, Shift finer

  1. 1Your turn Drag the pen toward a corner of the boardWith S 40 cm, Fig. 6(a)'s average tap error is 4, 1.3, 1.1 and 1.2 cm on 41, 61, 81 and 101 cm boards. On B 101 cm with S 80 cm, it is 5.1 cm within 20 cm of the centre and up to 18.4 cm beyond.
  2. 2Your turn Use the paper's 101 cm boardThe paper tests the sensor distance and the distance to the centre on a 101 cm board. Here the sensors start 40 cm apart.
  3. 3Your turn Spread the sensors to 80 cmOn the 101 cm board, Fig. 6(b)'s average tap error grows from 1.2 to 4.4 cm as S goes from 40 to 80 cm. One calibrated speed fits a larger area of uneven plywood less well.
  4. 4Your turn Swipe faster than 10 cm/sThe paper keeps the pen at 10 cm/s with a metronome. A faster pen moves farther in each 0.02 s segment, so each swipe has fewer segments.

Go Beyond the Paper · 2 of 3

Physical conditions

Question Which physical condition changes the tap and swipe errors most?The paper tests five materials, damped and undamped edges, and three instruments, all at 25 kHz. It gives no noise level: ours is assumed, a tap at the centre 34 dB over the noise.

You change
the instrument, the material, the edges and the noise

drag the pen on the board · the wheel moves it 5 mm, Shift finer

  1. 1Your turn Choose the instrumentTable 1 swipes damped wood with a pen cap, a fingernail and a metal bar: medium, light and heavy swipes. The hand holds the one you choose. The model makes a light swipe's pulses weaker and a heavy one's stronger (assumed).
    Instrument
  2. 2Your turn Change the material to stoneEach material has its own speeds and its own best band. Calibration finds both again on each board, so the tap error stays low on all five (Fig. 5).
  3. 3Your turn Damp the board's edgesThe weights soak up the wave before it reaches the edge. On wood, iron, cement and stone the paper's swipes then read closer to their true length; on ceramic it finds the opposite (Fig. 10).
  4. 4Your turn Lower the tap's SNR to 15 dBSNR: a centre tap's peak at a sensor over the noise, on the baseline board. The paper says that far from the centre the first peak decays to the noise level and cannot be detected (§5.2.5).

Optimal array setup design

Question Where should the geophones go, and how many?Each pair of geophones puts the tap on one hyperbola; the tap is where the hyperbolas cross. Two geophones give one hyperbola, so a 2-D fix needs three or more.

Fixed
the 101 cm wooden board, calibrated, a pen
You change
where the geophones are, and how many
You watch
the mean error over the test chosen, Fig. 3(b), (c) or (d)
  1. 1Your turn Choose a test of Fig. 3Fig. 3(b): 16 tap places in the central 40 cm square, each tapped 10 times (Fig. 4). Fig. 3(c): 20 cm swipes through the centre in eight directions, each swiped 10 times (§5.1.3). Fig. 3(d): taps and swipes over an 80 cm area, the geophones 80 cm apart.
    Test
  2. 2Your turn PressFor taps in the central 40 cm square (Fig. 3(b)), the paper's mean error rose from 1.2 cm at S = 40 cm to 4.4 cm at S = 80 cm. Over Fig. 3(d)'s 80 cm area: 5.1 cm within 20 cm of the centre, up to 18.4 cm beyond.
  3. 3Your turn Drag a geophone to a new place.
  4. 4Your turn PressFour more geophones, one at the middle of each side: the paper says denser sensors can cover a larger area (§6.2).
  5. 5Your turn Drag geophones off the board until two are left.Two geophones give one hyperbola: a line of places, not a point. The page then says there is no 2-D fix.
  6. 6Your turn PressBack to the paper's layout: S1 to S4 at the corners of a 40 cm square (Fig. 3(a)), on the 101 cm board (§5.1.2).
